passage:
The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. The Pellows, who farmed the place before her father, had built it with a through-stone every yard, and her tractor had passed it for thirty years without a scrape. What caused the collapse was frost. A hard January had lifted the stones at its base, and her ram stood in the gap as if he owned it.

Dell Haskett drove up from the fencing yard in Orley with wire in his truck and the cost written on a card. He said his fence posts went in below any frost and would hold a ram. Maren heard him out, then walked him down to the stream, where a row of old posts stood black and soft at the water's edge. On the way back she made her choice. She called his price fair, said she had all the help she needed, and pointed at me. That was how I came to join the work.

At first I thought the job was mostly lifting. Maren taught me to lay each stone with its length running into the wall, to pack the hearting tight, and to lean both faces in toward each other. When my fingers went numb she sent me to brush pitch onto the new gatepost, and I learned that a black, sticky job can also be the warm one.

By March the gap was one capstone short. Maren set the last one, stepped back, and balanced her wool hat on top of it. "Now it is the best-dressed wall in the parish," she said. She made me shake hands with it, and the two of us stood in the sleet laughing until the ram wandered up to look.

Maren called it the hardest winter in ten years, and I spent most of it kneeling in mud. What I took away was the ability to read a wall. When I pass one now I look for the through-stones and the lean of the faces, and I can tell within a yard where the frost will find it next.

The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. The Pellows, who farmed the place before her father, had built it with a through-stone every yard, and it had stood through every frost since. What caused the collapse was her ram. He had taken to climbing it to reach the ewes next door, and one November night he pulled the top stones down after him and the rest followed.

Maren had seen the fencing prices in the Orley paper. By the time Dell Haskett drove up from the yard with wire in his truck, she had already sorted the fallen stone into piles along the grass, and her choice was plain to see. He walked the gap with her, promising fence posts set below the frost and wire that would hold any ram, and she agreed that it would. She heard out the cost, thanked him, and sent him home with his card.

My mother put me on the Friday bus to join her, and at first I thought Maren was being stubborn over a few dollars. The gap ran up the steepest pitch of the field, where the tractor could barely climb, so we carried the stone up by hand. She showed me how to lay each one with its length running into the wall, and I learned to keep my back straight on the slope.

In March the gap was one capstone short. Maren set the last one, then took the carpenter's pencil from behind her ear and turned to me. "Half of these stones came up that slope on your back, and I want your name written under this one," she said. She tipped the cap up, and I wrote my name on its underside.

It was a hard winter, and we worked through most of it while the stream froze and thawed below us. When the bill for the new gate came in April, Maren paid it in coins from a jar on the windowsill, counting them twice. I understood then what Haskett's card would have meant to her that year.

The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. Her father had built that stretch himself the year she was born. Her tractor kept well clear of it, the stream ran thirty yards below, and the old Pellow walls on either side stood straight.

Dell Haskett drove up from the fencing yard in Orley with wire in his truck and the cost written on a card. He blamed the frost, as if that settled it, and said his posts would stand through any winter. Maren barely listened. She was turning over fallen stones, and when he asked for her choice she said she would ring him. After he left she asked aloud why this stretch had collapsed when its neighbours were upright.

So I joined her on weekends, and we took the rest of the stretch down to its footings. Maren tapped each stone with a hammer and listened to the pitch it gave back, a clear ring for a sound stone and a dull note for a cracked one, and I learned to hear the difference. The fault was in the building: her father had laid the two faces side by side with only rubble between them, and there was not one through-stone in the whole length.

By March the new stretch had a through-stone every yard and was one capstone short. Maren set the last one, then went along the line pressing each cap with both hands, feeling for the slightest wobble. "Keep the ewes out of this field until the frost is gone, because a new wall needs a month to settle," she said. That night she tied a rope across the gateway and went out twice with a torch to check it.

At first I had taken a wall for a pile of stones, and that hard winter taught me otherwise. Haskett's price was lower than she had expected, but she rang to turn him down while she watched her ram pacing the lower field, a heavy Dunmore tup that had walked through two wire fences before she bought him.

passage:
The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. The Pellows, who farmed the place before her father, had built it with a through-stone every yard. What caused the collapse was her own tractor. Backing a trailer of hay in the November dark, she caught the end of the wall, and the whole run went down behind it like a shelf of books.

Dell Haskett drove up from the fencing yard in Orley with wire in his truck and a cost lower than her feed bill, and I was on his side before he finished. His fence would go up in two days, it would hold her ram, and it would stand well back from the stream. Maren listened, then walked him to the gate, where a post he had set for the Dunmores two winters before leaned a hand's width out of the frost-hard ground. She said she would think about her choice. I thought she was being sentimental about a heap of rocks.

So I joined her every Saturday, grudgingly, with Haskett's pitch about two-day fences still running through my head. It lasted about a month. Somewhere between learning to set a through-stone and learning to pack the hearting, I began to see the wall as she did: a thing that would outlast us both, built from what the field had already given.

In March the gap was one capstone short. Maren set the last one and kept her hand on it, looking down at the empty lower field. "When I was your age there were forty ewes on that slope, and now there are eleven and one ram," she said. She stood there with her hand on the stone until the light was gone.

That hard winter put me on the other side of the argument for good. In April, riding the bus past the fence Haskett had put up along the Orley road, I counted three posts already leaning out of the thawed ground, and I found I preferred my aunt's wall to every yard of his wire.

passage:
The winter I turned fifteen, forty feet of the wall above my aunt Maren's top field lay in the grass. Her father had built it the year she was born, with a through-stone every yard. What caused the collapse was the stream. After the October rains it jumped its bank and ran along the foot of the wall for three days, washing away the footing until the face folded into the water.

Dell Haskett drove up from the fencing yard in Orley with wire in his truck and a cost she could meet, and as he talked he kept glancing at the sky to the north. His fence posts would stand well up the slope from the stream and hold any ram, he said, but she had a fortnight before the frost. "After that, nobody digs a post hole up here until March." The geese had been going over all week, and the air already smelled of snow. Maren said she would make her choice by Sunday.

On Sunday she brought out her father's old notebook, with a sketch of every stone in that stretch, and handed Haskett's card back to him at the gate. I joined her that afternoon. The only flat ground near the gap was the end of the village football pitch, so we sorted the stones there, hauled up from the stream bed by the tractor, and laid them out in his order.

Snow stopped us four weekends running, and by March the gap was still one capstone short. Maren set the last one just as Haskett's truck slowed on the road below, and he leaned out to call that she could have saved herself a winter. "You tried to rush me with your fortnight, and I want you off my road," she called down, and turned her back on the truck.

It was the hardest winter in ten years. At first I thought we would give up by Christmas, and some mornings I learned more about cold than about stone. But we kept on, a few stones at a time, through sleet and frozen wind, and the wall stood whole before the ground thawed.

passage:
In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Half the posts had rotted to stumps, and the commissioners wanted to know whether Rudd's line was still true.

Measuring from the tower of Sallow church, Varne found Rudd's posts standing in dry pasture a quarter of a mile above the nearest reeds, with sheep grazing around them. Year by year the river's silt had built the marsh outward. He drove his own cedar stakes along the line of dried reeds, while his chainman, Jonah Pell, followed in the punt.

Varne carried a first draft of the map, and at every stake he waited until a farmer and a reed-cutter had read it side by side. Through July both sides walked the line with him, arguing loudest where the creek bent, and by August every stake had been seen by a man from each.

The line ended at Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel. When Pell asked whose initials he should cut on the stake there, Varne handed him the knife. "Cut yours above mine, Jonah, because you carried the chain over every rod of this marsh."

That autumn the highest tides rose to the cedar stakes and stopped, as the reeds had said they would. In November farmers and reed-cutters signed the map together, and the quarrel that had outlasted Rudd ended with it. The commissioners hung the map in the Wexcombe courthouse, where Varne's line can still be read.

In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Half the posts had rotted to stumps, and the commissioners wanted to know whether Rudd's line was still true.

Measuring from the tower of Sallow church, Varne walked Rudd's line twice. Every post stood out on soft ground below the firm pasture, giving each farmer a strip of marsh, and in his book Varne listed the farmers who had paid Rudd's fee. He drove his own stakes along the bank of the creek, while his chainman, Jonah Pell, followed in the punt.

In October the commissioners heard his report in the Wexcombe courthouse, where a cold draft from a cracked pane kept lifting the corners of his map. A creek, they said, wandered with every high tide, and a boundary laid along one would be argued over again within ten years. Varne answered that Rudd's posts had been argued over for eighty.

They sent him back to Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel, to show them the end of his line. There Pell asked whether the stake might go on a dry hummock up the bank, his third such request that week. Varne pointed at the water. "Set it in the water where the chain ended, Jonah, and stop asking me to move the line."

In December the commissioners set Varne's map aside and ordered Rudd's posts renewed in oak where they stood. The farmers kept their strip, the reed-cutters kept their grievance, and the quarrel went on. Varne's map lay rolled in a courthouse drawer for forty years.

In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Half the posts had rotted to stumps, and the commissioners wanted to know whether Rudd's line was still true.

Measuring from the tower of Sallow church, Varne found Rudd's posts still standing among the reeds of the marsh. The first post he tested took his iron rod to the hand like wet bread, and so did the next two, after which he stopped testing them. He drove his own stakes along the edge of the open mud instead.

The mud would swallow a horse to its belly, so he and his chainman, Jonah Pell, worked it from a punt with so shallow a draft that it floated in a hand's depth of water. Pell poled while Varne sighted along the chain from the bow, and they set each stake while the mud lay bare.

The stake at Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel, was the last before the equinox. Pell asked whether it could stand like the others at the mud's edge. Varne had him drive it deeper and lash a second stake behind it. "The equinox tide comes in three days, and it will run higher than any tide we have seen here."

Three days later the tide took every stake on the mud, the doubled one at Gull Point with the rest. Varne spent the winter redrawing the whole map from his notebook, and in April he and Pell set the line again. The commissioners adopted that second map, though the farmers and reed-cutters went on quarreling over its edge.

In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Half the posts had rotted to stumps, and the commissioners wanted to know whether Rudd's line was still true.

Measuring from the tower of Sallow church, Varne found each of Rudd's surviving posts standing in freshly turned earth at the marsh's edge, a few yards nearer the farms than the rotted stumps of the row, and the only path to them ran from the reed-cutters' landing. He drove his own stakes along the place where the samphire stopped growing.

In June the militia draft took his second chainman, and Jonah Pell, who had only carried the far end of the chain, had to learn the whole work. Varne taught him to plumb the staff, count the links aloud and sight from stake to stake, and by August Pell was running long lengths of the line alone while Varne checked his figures from the punt.

Pell set the stake at Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel, and asked whether the iron stub beside it was one of Rudd's. Varne knelt and held it for a long while. "That is all that is left of the stake my father drove here, the spring before the river took him."

In October Varne's eyes failed him, and Pell finished the survey alone, carrying the line to the sea wall in the first frosts. The winter tides left every stake standing. The commissioners accepted the map in Pell's hand, with Varne's name above his own, and the farmers and reed-cutters went on quarreling as before.

In the spring of 1852 the commissioners of Wexcombe County hired Thaddeus Varne, a self-taught surveyor from the canal country, to fix the boundary of Sallow Marsh. Between the farmers' old sea wall and the open mud lay a mile of marsh, cut by a winding creek, fringed with samphire, and marked each spring by a line of dried reeds where the highest tides had stopped. For a generation the farmers and the reed-cutters had quarreled over its edge, and both sides accused each other of moving the oak posts that Amos Rudd, paid by the farmers, had set eighty years before. Varne spent his first week in the punt with his chainman, Jonah Pell, poling the creek and walking the length of the sea wall before he drove a single stake. Rudd's posts ran along the foot of the wall, where the marsh began, a dozen of them still sound, and the reed-cutters swore every one had crept seaward.

For his fixed point he chose the iron weathercock of Sallow church, the one mark visible from every channel of the delta, and he measured from it to each sound post while the sexton brought him a draft of cider in the tower. Every post stood within an inch of where Rudd's old field book put it, and Varne drove his own stakes along the foot of the sea wall beside them.

The last stake went in at Gull Point, where the creek meets the main channel, and a grey heron was standing on the very spot. Pell asked whether he should chase the bird off and set the stake. Varne laughed. "Let him finish his fishing first, Jonah, since he was surveying this point long before either of us."

The commissioners entered Varne's map in the county book as proof of Rudd's line and had the rotted posts renewed in oak in their old holes. His survey had shown that Rudd's line was right all along, though the reed-cutters still carried their quarrel to the courts.
